## 4. The collapse of the hierarchy

We now leave the reveal step behind and analyse the search step in the abstract.

### 4.1 The upper side: pigeonhole

**Theorem 4.1 (Birthday bound, upper side).** *Let $p \ge 1$, let $S$ be a finite search space with $p < |S|$, and let $f$ be any residue map with $f(x) < p$ for all $x$. Then there exist $x, y \in S$ with $x \neq y$ and $f(x) = f(y)$.*

*Proof.* $f$ maps $S$ into the $p$-element set $\{0, \dots, p-1\}$ and $|S| > p$, so $f$ is not injective on $S$. $\square$

**Theorem 4.2 (Structured value sets).** *Let $S$ be a finite search space, $B$ a finite set of naturals, and $f$ a map with $f(x) \in B$ for all $x \in S$. If $|B| < |S|$, then $f$ has a collision on $S$.*

Theorem 4.2 is the general form: the collision threshold is the size of the **value set**, whatever it happens to be. Theorem 4.1 is the case $B = \{0,\dots,p-1\}$. The "structured evaluation" row of the hierarchy — schemes whose values are confined to a set of size roughly $p/h$ for some structural parameter $h$ (for example an evaluation indexed by a class group of class number $h$) — is the case $|B| \approx p/h$, and Theorem 4.2 says such a scheme collides after only $|B| + 1$ evaluations, a genuine factor-$h$ improvement in *evaluation count*. Section 7 shows why this improvement is nonetheless confined.

### 4.2 The lower side: an adversary

**Theorem 4.3 (Birthday bound, lower side).** *Let $p \ge 1$ and let $S$ be a finite search space with $|S| \le p$. Then there exists a residue map $f$ with $f(x) < p$ for all $x$, which is injective on $S$.*

*Proof.* Since $|S| \le p$, there is an injection $e$ from $S$ into a $p$-element set, which we identify with $\{0, \dots, p-1\}$. Define $f(x) = e(x)$ for $x \in S$ and $f(x) = 0$ otherwise. Then $f(x) < p$ everywhere (using $p \ge 1$ for the default value), and $f$ restricted to $S$ is $e$, hence injective. $\square$

The importance of Theorem 4.3 is methodological. Without it, "the scheme needs more than $p$ tuples" would be a statement about one particular analysis. With it, the statement becomes a theorem about *all possible* schemes of this shape: for $|S| \le p$ there is a concrete residue assignment defeating the scheme.

### 4.3 The collapse

**Theorem 4.4 (Collapse of the birthday-bound hierarchy).** *Let $p \ge 1$ and let $S$ be a finite search space. Then*
$$ S \text{ guarantees collisions modulo } p \qquad \Longleftrightarrow \qquad p < |S|. $$

*Proof.* ($\Leftarrow$) is Theorem 4.1. ($\Rightarrow$): suppose the guarantee holds but $|S| \le p$. By Theorem 4.3 there is a residue map $f$ into $\{0,\dots,p-1\}$ injective on $S$. By the guarantee, $f$ has a collision $x \ne y$ on $S$ with $f(x)=f(y)$; injectivity gives $x = y$, a contradiction. $\square$

**Corollary 4.5 (Exact threshold).** *$S$ guarantees collisions modulo $p$ if and only if $|S| \ge p+1$.*

**Discussion.** Theorem 4.4 is deliberately unimpressive as a piece of mathematics and consequential as a piece of accounting. Its criterion is a statement about $|S|$ alone. It is blind to:

- the **arity** $r$ of the scheme;
- the way $S$ is *generated* — as $A^r$ for a stored set $A$, as a class-group orbit, as anything;
- the **additive structure** of the underlying numbers;
- the particular residue map, since the criterion quantifies over all of them.

Consequently every row of the hierarchy table has the same entry in the "objects inspected" column: $p+1$. What differs between rows is only the *generation cost*: how few stored elements suffice to name a search space of that size. Arity $r$ buys storage $|A| \approx p^{1/r}$, and nothing else.

### 4.4 The $r$-SUM instance

**Definition 4.6 (Tuple space).** For $r \ge 0$ and a finite set $A$ of naturals, the *$r$-tuple space* $T_r(A)$ is the set of all functions from $\{1,\dots,r\}$ to $A$. Its cardinality is $|A|^r$.

**Theorem 4.7 ($r$-SUM collision).** *Let $p \ge 1$, let $A$ be finite with $|A| = k$, and suppose $p < k^r$. Then there exist distinct $u, v \in T_r(A)$ with*
$$ \sum_{i=1}^r u_i \;\equiv\; \sum_{i=1}^r v_i \pmod p. $$

*Proof.* Apply Theorem 4.1 with $S = T_r(A)$, of cardinality $k^r > p$, and the residue map $u \mapsto \bigl(\sum_i u_i\bigr) \bmod p$. $\square$

For $r = 2$ this is the sumset collision $a + b \equiv c+d$; for $r=3$ the $3$SUM collision $a+b+c \equiv d+e+f$.

**Theorem 4.8 ($r$-SUM adversary).** *If $k^r \le p$ there is a residue map into $\{0,\dots,p-1\}$ injective on $T_r(A)$: no $r$-SUM scheme with $|A| = k$ can be guaranteed to collide.*

**Corollary 4.9 (Storage monotonicity).** *If $k \ge 1$, $r \le r'$, and $p < k^r$, then $p < k^{r'}$. Raising the arity never increases the storage requirement.*

Corollary 4.9 is the *only* sense in which the hierarchy is real, and we state it explicitly to make the contrast exact.

### 4.5 A quantitative snapshot: $p = 997$

**Proposition 4.10.** *For every natural $k$:*
$$ 997 < k^3 \iff k \ge 10, \qquad\qquad 997 < k^2 \iff k \ge 32. $$

*Proof.* $9^3 = 729 \le 997 < 1000 = 10^3$ and $31^2 = 961 \le 997 < 1024 = 32^2$; monotonicity of $k \mapsto k^m$ does the rest. $\square$

**Corollary 4.11 (The exponent gap, and its emptiness).** *At $p = 997$ the $3$SUM scheme requires $10$ stored elements where the sumset scheme requires $32$ — a $3.2\times$ improvement in storage, the promised $p^{1/2} \to p^{1/3}$. Yet the inspected search spaces are $10^3 = 1000$ and $32^2 = 1024$, both exceeding $997$ by the smallest possible margin, and differing from each other by $2.4\%$.*

The two schemes do the same work. One of them merely remembers less while doing it.

---

## 5. The $\sqrt N$ barrier

**Lemma 5.1.** *If $q \le p$ then $\lfloor\sqrt{pq}\rfloor \le p$.*

*Proof.* $pq \le p^2$, so $\lfloor\sqrt{pq}\rfloor \le \lfloor\sqrt{p^2}\rfloor = p$. $\square$

**Theorem 5.2 (Arity-independent cost barrier).** *Let $N = pq$ with $q \le p$ and $p \ge 1$. If a search space $S$ guarantees collisions modulo $p$, then*
$$ |S| > \lfloor\sqrt{N}\rfloor. $$

*Proof.* Theorem 4.4 gives $|S| > p$, and Lemma 5.1 gives $p \ge \lfloor\sqrt N\rfloor$. $\square$

**Corollary 5.3 ($r$-SUM barrier).** *For any arity $r$ and any $A$ with $p < |A|^r$ and $q \le p$, we have $|A|^r > \lfloor\sqrt{pq}\rfloor$: a guaranteed $r$-SUM scheme inspects more than $\sqrt N$ tuples.*

This is the paper's headline negative result, and it is worth being precise about what it does and does not say.

*It does say:* no scheme in this family — of any arity, over any set of integers, with any generation rule — can be *guaranteed* to find a collision modulo the larger prime factor of $N$ while inspecting at most $\sqrt N$ objects. The bound is unconditional, non-asymptotic and non-probabilistic.

*It does not say:* that factoring requires $\sqrt N$ work. It says that *this family of methods* does. Sieve methods do not proceed by waiting for a residue collision in a search space, and are not subject to Theorem 5.2. The theorem's value is precisely that it draws the boundary of the collision paradigm sharply enough to say where one must leave it.

---

## 6. The amplitude barrier

Theorem 5.2 counts objects. We now show a completely different quantity is also stuck at $\sqrt N$: the *arithmetic size* of the integers a scheme manipulates. This obstruction is invisible to the counting analysis, and it applies even to schemes that inspect infinitely many tuples.

**Definition 6.1 (Sum set of a tuple space).** For $r \ge 0$ and finite $A$, let
$$ \Sigma_r(A) \;=\; \Bigl\{ \textstyle\sum_{i=1}^r u_i \;:\; u \in T_r(A) \Bigr\}, $$
the set of *distinct integer values* achieved as $r$-tuple sums.

**Lemma 6.2.** *If every $a \in A$ satisfies $a \le M$, then every $s \in \Sigma_r(A)$ satisfies $s \le rM$.*

**Theorem 6.3 (Amplitude bound).** *If $A \subseteq [1, M]$, then $|\Sigma_r(A)| \le rM + 1$, however large $|A|^r$ may be.*

*Proof.* By Lemma 6.2, $\Sigma_r(A) \subseteq \{0,1,\dots,rM\}$. $\square$

**Theorem 6.4 (All collisions trivial when entries are small).** *Let $A \subseteq [1,M]$ and suppose $rM < p$. Then for any $u, v \in T_r(A)$ with $\sum_i u_i \equiv \sum_i v_i \pmod p$, one has $\sum_i u_i = \sum_i v_i$.*

*Proof.* Suppose without loss of generality $\sum u_i < \sum v_i$. The congruence gives $p \mid \sum v_i - \sum u_i$, and this difference is positive, hence $\ge p$. But both sums lie in $[0, rM]$, so the difference is at most $rM < p$ — contradiction. $\square$

**Corollary 6.5 (Amplitude barrier).** *A scheme with $A \subseteq [1,M]$ and $rM < p$ cannot factor $N = pq$ by collision, no matter how many tuples it inspects: every collision it finds has difference $0$, and the reveal step returns $\gcd(0, N) = N$, never a proper factor. Success therefore requires $p \le rM$, i.e. entries of size at least $p/r \ge \sqrt N / r$.*

**Remark 6.6 (Structure cannot help).** Theorem 6.3 depends only on the interval $[1,M]$ containing $A$ — never on $A$'s additive structure. Sidon sets, geometric progressions, smooth-number sets, and any other additive-combinatorial device produce sums confined to the same interval and are therefore subject to the same bound. This is a sharp limitation on a natural line of attack: one cannot arrange for a small-entry set to have an unusually rich modular image, because the *integer* image is capped by amplitude alone.

**Remark 6.7 (The bound is nearly attained).** Theorem 6.3 gives the necessary condition $p \le rM$. For the full interval $A = \{1,\dots,M\}$ the sum set is exactly $\{r, r+1, \dots, rM\}$, of size $r(M-1)+1$, so the counting condition $p < |\Sigma_r(A)|$ holds precisely when $M \ge p/r + 1$. The two conditions differ by a single additive step, so the amplitude bound is essentially attained rather than lossy. For $r = 3$ this predicts the smallest workable entry bound $M = \lceil p/3\rceil + 1$, i.e. $M = 5$ at $p = 11$ and $M = 35$ at $p = 101$ — values confirmed by direct enumeration.

---

## 7. The span and coverage barriers

The previous sections analysed specific generation rules. We now abstract entirely.

**Definition 7.1 (Abstract collision scheme).** A *scheme* consists of a finite **search space** $S$ (whose cardinality $k = |S|$ is the scheme's cost) together with a **value map** $v : S \to \mathbb{N}$. Its **difference set** is
$$ D \;=\; \{\, v(x) - v(y) \;:\; x, y \in S,\; v(x)\ge v(y) \,\}, $$
and the scheme **reveals** $f$ from $N$ if some $d \in D$ has $d > 0$ and $\gcd(d, N) = f$.

**Lemma 7.2.** *$|D| \le k^2$.*

This definition is deliberately permissive. It covers sumset, $3$SUM, $r$-SUM, structured evaluation schemes, and anything else whose output is "take a $\gcd$ of a difference of two computed numbers with $N$". Whatever is proved about it applies to all of them at once.

### 7.1 Span

**Theorem 7.3 (Span barrier).** *If a scheme reveals $f$ from $N$, then some $d \in D$ satisfies $d \ge f$.*

*Proof.* Take $d \in D$ with $d > 0$ and $\gcd(d, N) = f$. Then $f \mid d$ and $d > 0$, so $f \le d$. $\square$

**Corollary 7.4 ($\sqrt N$ form).** *If $N = pq$ with $q \le p$ and a scheme reveals $p$, then two of its values differ by at least $\lfloor\sqrt N\rfloor$; in particular its largest value is at least $\lfloor \sqrt N\rfloor$.*

**Corollary 7.5 (Small values never factor).** *If all values of a scheme are $< B$ and $B \le p$, the scheme cannot reveal $p$ from $N = pq$.*

*Proof.* All differences are $< B \le p$, contradicting Theorem 7.3. $\square$

A cleaner special case, in the same spirit but stated for integer value sets directly:

**Theorem 7.6 (Interval span barrier).** *If all values of a scheme lie in an interval $[L, L+p)$, then any two congruent values modulo $p$ are equal. Consequently no useful collision exists, and the value range must be at least $p$.*

**Remark 7.7 (Structure improves counting, never span).** Return to the structured-evaluation row. By Theorem 4.2, confining values to a set $B$ with $|B| \approx p/h$ makes collisions appear after only $|B| + 1$ evaluations — a genuine factor-$h$ saving over the generic $p+1$. But Theorem 7.3 is untouched by this: the revealed factor $p$ still forces two *integer values at distance at least $p$*. Structure compresses the number of objects; it cannot compress the objects. This is a clean separation between two resources that the naive cost accounting conflates.

### 7.2 Coverage

Could a single fixed scheme — a fixed table of numbers, computed once — factor many different semiprimes? The next bound says no, by pure counting on prime divisors.

**Lemma 7.8.** *Let $Q$ be a finite set of distinct primes, all $\ge P$, all dividing a positive integer $d$. Then $P^{|Q|} \le d$.*

*Proof.* The primes are distinct, so their product divides $d$; the product is at least $P^{|Q|}$; and $d > 0$. $\square$

**Corollary 7.9.** *If $P > 1$ and $d > 0$, then $d$ has at most $\log_P d$ distinct prime divisors $\ge P$.*

**Theorem 7.10 (Coverage barrier).** *Let a scheme have $k$ search points and let $Q$ be a set of primes such that every $p \in Q$ satisfies $p \ge P > 1$ and divides some difference $d \in D$ with $0 < d \le B$. Then*
$$ |Q| \;\le\; \log_P(B)\cdot k^2. $$

*Proof sketch.* Choose for each $p \in Q$ a witnessing difference $g(p) \in D$ with $0 < g(p) \le B$ and $p \mid g(p)$. The image $g(Q)$ is contained in $D$, so $|g(Q)| \le k^2$ by Lemma 7.2. Each fibre $g^{-1}(b)$ consists of distinct primes $\ge P$ all dividing the single positive integer $b \le B$, so by Corollary 7.9 and monotonicity of the logarithm, $|g^{-1}(b)| \le \log_P b \le \log_P B$. Summing over fibres, $|Q| \le \log_P(B)\cdot|g(Q)| \le \log_P(B)\cdot k^2$. $\square$

**Corollary 7.11 (Cost form).** *A scheme required to reveal each of $T$ distinct primes $\ge P$, with all differences bounded by $B$, must have search space size $k$ satisfying $T \le \log_P(B)\cdot k^2$, i.e.*
$$ k \;\ge\; \sqrt{T / \log_P B}. $$

The significance of Theorem 7.10 is that it is a *non-uniformity* bound: it limits what precomputation can achieve. Whereas Theorem 5.2 says a scheme is slow on each input, Theorem 7.10 says a scheme cannot be reused across inputs. Together they close the two obvious escape routes.

---

## 8. The positive theorem: collision factoring, certified

We now assemble the pieces. The following says that the two barriers are not merely necessary but, once cleared, sufficient.

**Theorem 8.1 (Master theorem for $r$-SUM collision factoring).** *Let $N = pq$ with $p, q$ prime. Let $A$ be a finite set of positive integers with $a \le M$ for all $a \in A$, and suppose*

1. *(amplitude) $rM < N$, and*
2. *(counting) $p < |\Sigma_r(A)|$.*

*Then there exist $s, t \in \Sigma_r(A)$ with $t < s$ and*
$$ \gcd(s - t,\, N) \;=\; p. $$

*Proof.* Since $|\Sigma_r(A)| > p$, the map $x \mapsto x \bmod p$ cannot be injective on $\Sigma_r(A)$; pick $s \ne t$ in $\Sigma_r(A)$ with $s \equiv t \pmod p$ and, relabelling, $t < s$. Then $p \mid s - t$. Also $s \le rM < N$ by Lemma 6.2 and hypothesis 1. Corollary 3.6 gives $\gcd(s-t, N) = p$. $\square$

**Corollary 8.2 ($3$SUM instance).** *With $r = 3$: if $A \subseteq [1,M]$ with $3M < N$ and the triple-sum set $\Sigma_3(A)$ has more than $p$ elements, then two achieved triple sums differ by a quantity whose $\gcd$ with $N$ is exactly $p$.*

**Theorem 8.3 (Both barriers are necessary).** *Let $q \le p$, let $A \subseteq [1, M]$, and suppose $p < |\Sigma_r(A)|$ (so that a useful collision is guaranteed). Then*

1. $p \le rM$ *— the entries must have size at least $p/r$; and*
2. $|A|^r > \lfloor\sqrt{pq}\rfloor$ *— the tuple count exceeds $\sqrt N$.*

*Proof.* (1) By Theorem 6.3, $|\Sigma_r(A)| \le rM+1$; combined with $p < |\Sigma_r(A)|$ this gives $p < rM+1$, i.e. $p \le rM$. (2) $\Sigma_r(A)$ is an image of $T_r(A)$, so $|\Sigma_r(A)| \le |A|^r$, whence $p < |A|^r$; now apply Corollary 5.3. $\square$

**Corollary 8.4 ($3$SUM cost profile).** *A $3$SUM scheme against $N = pq$ with $q \le p$ requires entries of size at least $p/3$ and inspects more than $\lfloor\sqrt N\rfloor$ triples. Both costs are $\Omega(\sqrt N)$.*

This is the final accounting. The exponent improvement $p^{1/2} \to p^{1/3}$ is real, it is confined to storage, and every other resource stays at $\sqrt N$.

---

## 9. Algorithms

We record the two procedures the theory certifies, with their complexities.

### 9.1 Sum-set collision factoring

**Input:** a semiprime $N$, an arity $r$, an entry bound $M$.
**Output:** a nontrivial factor of $N$, or failure.

1. Choose $A \subseteq [1, M]$.
2. Enumerate $\Sigma_r(A)$, maintaining a dictionary from residues modulo a *guessed* modulus — or, in practice, maintain the achieved sums themselves and sort.
3. For each pair of achieved sums $t < s$, compute $g = \gcd(s - t, N)$.
4. If $1 < g < N$, output $g$.

By Theorem 8.1, if $rM < N$ and $|\Sigma_r(A)| > p$, step 4 succeeds. By Theorem 8.3, this requires $M \ge p/r$ and more than $\sqrt N$ inspected tuples, so the procedure is $\Omega(\sqrt N)$ and — with sorting — $O(k^r \log k^r)$ where $k = |A|$.

Note a subtlety the theory clarifies: one does not need to know $p$ to run the algorithm. The residue structure modulo $p$ is invisible; only the $\gcd$ test at the end reveals whether a difference happened to be a multiple of $p$. The birthday bound guarantees that *some* pair works once the sum set exceeds $p$ in size.

### 9.2 Threshold and barrier calculator

Given $p$ (or a target $N$) and an arity $r$, one computes:

- the **storage threshold** $k^\ast(p, r) = \min\{k : k^r > p\} = \lfloor p^{1/r}\rfloor + 1$;
- the **work** $\bigl(k^\ast\bigr)^r$, which always exceeds $p$ and is within a small factor of it;
- the **amplitude threshold** $M^\ast(p,r) = \lceil p/r\rceil$ (necessary), attained by the full interval at $\lceil p/r\rceil + 1$;
- the **span requirement** $\lfloor\sqrt N\rfloor$.

The output is the hierarchy table for that instance, exhibiting the collapse numerically. This is the computation performed in the accompanying numerical study.

---

## 10. Applications and interpretation

**A bridge between problem families.** Corollary 3.4 makes precise the sense in which $3$SUM modulo an unknown prime is a factoring primitive. This is a bridge in the fine-grained complexity sense: an efficient algorithm for the modular variant of $3$SUM against adversarially hidden moduli would break factoring. The bridge is one-directional and, as our barriers show, load-limited; but it identifies a modular $3$SUM variant whose hardness is at least that of factoring at the $\sqrt N$ scale.

**A design principle for cost accounting.** The clearest methodological lesson is Corollary 4.11: an improvement in one resource (storage, $p^{1/2} \to p^{1/3}$) may be exactly compensated by no improvement at all in another (work, always $> p$). Because the collapse theorem is an *equivalence*, this is not a limitation of an analysis but a fact about the problem. Whenever a family of algorithms is parameterised by "how cleverly the search space is generated," it is worth asking whether the acceptance criterion depends on generation at all. Here it does not.

**Three barriers of different type.** It is unusual for a single $\Omega(\sqrt N)$ bound to be provable in three independent ways:

- *counting* (Theorem 5.2) — you must inspect many objects;
- *amplitude/span* (Corollary 6.5, Corollary 7.4) — the objects must themselves be large;
- *coverage* (Theorem 7.10) — one fixed set of objects cannot serve many inputs.

Each of these could in principle be circumvented separately; none of them can be circumvented by arity. That robustness is the reason we regard $\sqrt N$ as the true home of the collision paradigm rather than an artefact.

**What is not claimed.** None of this bears on the complexity of factoring itself. Sub-exponential methods exist and are not collision searches. The results here delimit a paradigm, and delimiting a paradigm crisply is useful precisely because it tells the algorithm designer where not to look.

---

## 11. Future directions

The framework above suggests three falsifiable conjectures.

**C1. Every $\gcd$-extraction scheme obeys a span–coverage trade-off.** For an abstract scheme with $k$ search points and values bounded by $B$ that reveals the larger factor of *every* semiprime $N = pq$ with $\sqrt N \in [P, 2P)$, one should have
$$ k^2 \cdot \log_P B \;\ge\; \pi(2P) - \pi(P), $$
hence $k \ge P^{1/2 - o(1)}$ — a $\sqrt N$ lower bound with no probabilistic or oracle assumptions. The coverage barrier (Theorem 7.10) already bounds the number of large primes a fixed value set can expose by $\log_P(B)\cdot k^2$; only a prime-counting input is needed to convert this into an unconditional cost bound.

**C2. Non-uniform sets do not beat the amplitude barrier.** For every finite $A \subseteq [1,M]$ and every arity $r$, the number of distinct residues modulo $p$ realised by $r$-tuple sums over $A$ should be at most $\min(rM+1,\, p)$, and the requirement $p \le rM$ for a guaranteed factor-revealing collision should be unimprovable by any choice of $A$ — Sidon sets, geometric progressions and smooth-number sets included. The amplitude bound depends only on the interval containing $A$, never on its additive structure, so additive-combinatorial cleverness cannot help. Because the measured interval thresholds match the predicted values exactly at small $p$ ($M = 5$ at $p = 11$, $M = 35$ at $p = 101$, both with $r = 3$), the conjecture is sharp and would be falsified by a single counterexample set.

**C3. Modular structure can beat the counting threshold but never the span.** For any scheme whose values are constrained to a structured residue set $B$ with $|B| \approx p/h$, collisions appear after $|B|+1$ evaluations, yet the revealed factor still forces two integer values at distance $\ge p$. Structure should therefore improve the collision *count* by the factor $h$ while leaving the arithmetic size of the manipulated objects untouched, since the span barrier constrains numerical values alone and is invariant under any change of indexing.

Beyond these, two directions seem worth pursuing. First, a *probabilistic* refinement: the collapse theorem is a worst-case guarantee, and the average-case birthday behaviour (collisions after $\Theta(\sqrt{p})$ random samples) deserves the same arity-independence analysis — we expect the same collapse, with $\sqrt p$ in place of $p$, and with the amplitude barrier unchanged. Second, an examination of whether any *non*-collision extraction rule (something other than $\gcd$ of a difference) evades Theorem 7.3, which would identify precisely which feature of the paradigm the span barrier punishes.

---

## 12. Conclusion

A single greatest-common-divisor computation converts a $3$SUM solution modulo a hidden prime into that prime, with no side conditions beyond smallness. This makes a family of collision-based factoring schemes available, apparently arranged in a hierarchy in which higher arity means a better exponent.

The hierarchy collapses. A collision is guaranteed exactly when the search space exceeds the modulus — a criterion in which the arity does not appear — so all schemes share the threshold $p+1$, and hence exceed $\sqrt N$. Two independent barriers reach the same magnitude for different reasons: the amplitude/span obstruction forces the manipulated integers to be of size $\sqrt N$, and the coverage obstruction forbids a fixed scheme from serving many inputs. Once both barriers are cleared, the method provably works.

The improvement from $p^{1/2}$ to $p^{1/3}$ is real, and it is an improvement in storage alone. The barrier does not move.

\begin{abstract}

scheme cannot factor at all; success forces $p\le rM$. The \emph{span barrier}:

\section{Introduction}

\subsection{Two problems, one bridge}

The \textbf{$3$SUM problem} asks, given a finite set $A$ of integers, whether
there exist $a,b,c\in A$ with $a+b+c=0$. It occupies a distinguished position
in fine-grained complexity: a large family of problems in computational
geometry and string algorithms is $3$SUM-hard, and the $3$SUM conjecture
anchors a web of conditional lower bounds.

\textbf{Integer factoring} asks, given $N$, for a nontrivial divisor. For
$N=pq$ a product of two primes of comparable size it is the canonical hardness
assumption of public-key cryptography.

These problems are not usually discussed together. We connect them in a
direction that is elementary to state: \emph{a $3$SUM instance taken modulo an
unknown prime factor of $N$ is a factoring oracle.} The connection runs through
a two-line lemma and a greatest-common-divisor computation. The interesting
mathematics lies not in the bridge but in the precise accounting of what
crossing it costs.

\subsection{The seductive hierarchy}

Once one accepts the reveal lemma, factoring $N=pq$ reduces to producing a
quantity below $N$ divisible by $p$. The birthday bound supplies such
quantities: generate more than $p$ integers and two are congruent modulo $p$;
their difference is a nonzero multiple of $p$. The design question is how to
generate many integers cheaply, and the natural answers form a ladder of
increasing arity.

\section{Notation}

All variables denote natural numbers unless stated otherwise. For a finite set
$S$, $\lvert S\rvert$ is its cardinality. For naturals with $b\le a$ we use
$a\equiv b \pmod p \iff p \mid a-b$, with $a-b$ the ordinary difference. We
write $\lfloor\sqrt N\rfloor$ for the integer square root; all inequalities
involving square roots are stated in this integer form and are exact, not
asymptotic. A \emph{semiprime} is $N=pq$ with $p,q$ prime; where a
\emph{larger factor} is meant, $q\le p$.

\begin{definition}[Residue map]
Given a finite \emph{search space} $S$ (a finite set of arbitrary objects) and
a modulus $p\ge 1$, a \emph{residue map} is a function $f$ into
$\{0,1,\dots,p-1\}$. A \emph{collision} for $f$ on $S$ is a pair $x,y\in S$
with $x\ne y$ and $f(x)=f(y)$.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Guaranteed collision]
$S$ \emph{guarantees collisions modulo $p$} if \emph{every} residue map into
$\{0,\dots,p-1\}$ admits a collision on $S$. This universal quantification is
the correct notion for a lower bound: a designer who does not know $p$ cannot
rely on a favourable $f$.
\end{definition}

\section{The reveal lemma}\label{sec:reveal}

\begin{theorem}[Factor reveal]\label{thm:reveal}
Let $p,q$ be primes, $N=pq$, and let $s$ satisfy $0<s<N$ and $p\mid s$. Then
$\gcd(s,N)=p$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Put $g=\gcd(s,N)$. Since $p\mid s$ and $p\mid N$ we have $p\mid g$; write
$g=pd$. From $g\mid pq$ and $p\ne 0$ we get $d\mid q$, so $d=1$ or $d=q$. If
$d=1$ then $g=p$. If $d=q$ then $g=N$, and $g\mid s$ gives $N\mid s$; with
$s>0$ this forces $s\ge N$, contradicting $s<N$.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}[A redundant hypothesis]
The literature usually adds the hypothesis $q\nmid s$, to exclude the case in
which the greatest common divisor returns $N$. The proof shows it is
\emph{implied by} $s<N$.
\end{remark}

\begin{proposition}[No double divisibility below $N$]\label{prop:double}
Let $p\ne q$ be primes and $0<s<pq$. Then not both $p\mid s$ and $q\mid s$.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
Coprimality upgrades the two divisibilities to $pq\mid s$, whence $s\ge pq$.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[$3$SUM reveal]\label{cor:3sum}
If $p,q$ are prime, $0<a+b+c<pq$, and $p\mid a+b+c$, then
$\gcd(a+b+c,\,pq)=p$.
\end{corollary}

\begin{corollary}[$r$-SUM reveal]
Let $I$ be a finite index set and $f:I\to\N$. If
$0<\sum_{i\in I}f(i)<pq$ and $p\mid\sum_{i\in I}f(i)$, then
$\gcd\bigl(\sum_{i\in I}f(i),\,pq\bigr)=p$.
\end{corollary}

The reveal phenomenon is thus not special to triples: the arity plays no role
in the reveal step. This is the first hint of the paper's theme.

\begin{corollary}[Collision reveal]\label{cor:colreveal}
Let $p,q$ be prime and $t<s<pq$ with $p\mid s-t$. Then $\gcd(s-t,\,pq)=p$.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
Apply Theorem~\ref{thm:reveal} to $s-t$, positive by $t<s$ and at most
$s<pq$.
\end{proof}

This is the shape actually produced by a search: not a sum divisible by $p$
(we cannot arrange that) but a \emph{difference of two sums}.

\begin{corollary}[Sumset collision]
If $c+d<a+b<pq$ and $(a+b)\equiv(c+d)\pmod p$, then
$\gcd\bigl((a+b)-(c+d),\,pq\bigr)=p$.
\end{corollary}

\begin{theorem}[$3$SUM collision dichotomy]
Let $p,q$ be prime and let two triples satisfy $a+b+c<pq$, $a'+b'+c'<pq$ and
$(a+b+c)\equiv(a'+b'+c')\pmod p$. Then either the integer sums are equal---the
collision is trivial and yields no information---or
$\gcd(\max-\min,\,pq)=p$, where $\max$ and $\min$ are the larger and smaller of
the two sums.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Trichotomy on the two sums; in the unequal case apply
Corollary~\ref{cor:colreveal}.
\end{proof}

This isolates the enemy: \textbf{trivial collisions}, where the integer sums
coincide. Section~\ref{sec:amplitude} shows this failure mode is a barrier, not
a nuisance.

\subsection{A complete census: \texorpdfstring{$N=143$}{N=143}}

Take $N=143=11\cdot 13$ and all triples $1\le a<b<c\le 12$. Every such triple
has $a+b+c\le 33<143$, so Theorem~\ref{thm:reveal} applies to all of them.

\begin{proposition}[Census]
Among the triples $1\le a<b<c\le 12$, exactly $20$ have $11\mid a+b+c$ and
$13\nmid a+b+c$, and exactly $0$ have both $11\mid a+b+c$ and $13\mid a+b+c$.
\end{proposition}

The second count is not an accident of the range: by
Proposition~\ref{prop:double} it is $0$ for \emph{every} range in which the
triple sums stay below $143$, in particular for all $1\le a<b<c\le n$ with
$3n<143$. The first count is range-dependent: restricting to
$1\le a<b<c\le 11$ leaves $15$ such triples.

\begin{corollary}
For every triple with $0<a+b+c<143$ and $11\mid a+b+c$ one has
$\gcd(a+b+c,143)=11$.
\end{corollary}

Thus $2+4+5=11$, $1+9+12=22$, $3+8+11=22$ and $10+11+12=33$ each factor $143$
on the spot. The method's failure mode has provably zero instances here.

\section{The collapse of the hierarchy}\label{sec:collapse}

\subsection{The upper side: pigeonhole}

\begin{theorem}[Birthday bound, upper side]\label{thm:pigeon}
Let $p\ge 1$, let $S$ be finite with $p<\lvert S\rvert$, and let $f$ be any
residue map with $f(x)<p$ for all $x$. Then $f$ has a collision on $S$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
$f$ maps $S$ into a set of $p$ elements and $\lvert S\rvert>p$, so $f$ is not
injective on $S$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Structured value sets]\label{thm:structured}
Let $S$ be finite, $B$ a finite set of naturals, and $f$ a map with
$f(x)\in B$ for all $x\in S$. If $\lvert B\rvert<\lvert S\rvert$, then $f$ has
a collision on $S$.
\end{theorem}

Theorem~\ref{thm:structured} is the general form: the collision threshold is
the size of the \emph{value set}, whatever it is. The structured-evaluation row
of the hierarchy---schemes confined to a value set of size roughly $p/h$ for a
structural parameter $h$, for instance an evaluation indexed by a class group
of class number $h$---collides after only $\lvert B\rvert+1$ evaluations, a
genuine factor-$h$ improvement in evaluation count.
Remark~\ref{rmk:structure} shows why the improvement is confined.

\subsection{The lower side: an adversary}

\begin{theorem}[Birthday bound, lower side]\label{thm:adv}
Let $p\ge 1$ and let $S$ be finite with $\lvert S\rvert\le p$. Then there is a
residue map $f$ with $f(x)<p$ for all $x$ that is injective on $S$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Since $\lvert S\rvert\le p$ there is an injection $e$ of $S$ into a
$p$-element set, identified with $\{0,\dots,p-1\}$. Set $f(x)=e(x)$ on $S$ and
$f(x)=0$ elsewhere; then $f(x)<p$ everywhere, using $p\ge 1$ for the default
value, and $f$ restricted to $S$ is injective.
\end{proof}

The importance of Theorem~\ref{thm:adv} is methodological: without it, ``the
scheme needs more than $p$ tuples'' would be a statement about one analysis.
With it, it becomes a theorem about all schemes of this shape.

\subsection{The collapse}

\begin{theorem}[Collapse of the birthday-bound hierarchy]\label{thm:collapse}
Let $p\ge 1$ and let $S$ be finite. Then $S$ guarantees collisions modulo $p$
if and only if $p<\lvert S\rvert$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
($\Leftarrow$) is Theorem~\ref{thm:pigeon}. ($\Rightarrow$): if the guarantee
holds and $\lvert S\rvert\le p$, Theorem~\ref{thm:adv} supplies a residue map
injective on $S$; the guarantee produces a collision $x\ne y$ with $f(x)=f(y)$,
and injectivity gives $x=y$, a contradiction.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Exact threshold]
$S$ guarantees collisions modulo $p$ if and only if $\lvert S\rvert\ge p+1$.
\end{corollary}

The criterion of Theorem~\ref{thm:collapse} is a statement about
$\lvert S\rvert$ alone. It is blind to the arity $r$; to the way $S$ is
\emph{generated}---as $A^r$ for a stored set $A$, as a class-group orbit, as
anything; to the additive structure of the underlying numbers; and to the
particular residue map, since the criterion quantifies over all of them.
Consequently every row of the hierarchy has the same entry in the ``objects
inspected'' column, namely $p+1$. What differs is only the \emph{generation
cost}: how few stored elements suffice to name a search space of that size.

\subsection{The \texorpdfstring{$r$-SUM}{r-SUM} instance}

\begin{definition}[Tuple space]
For $r\ge 0$ and finite $A\subseteq\N$, the \emph{$r$-tuple space} $T_r(A)$ is
the set of all functions $\{1,\dots,r\}\to A$; its cardinality is
$\lvert A\rvert^r$.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[$r$-SUM collision]\label{thm:rsum}
Let $p\ge 1$, $\lvert A\rvert=k$, and $p<k^r$. Then there are distinct
$u,v\in T_r(A)$ with $\sum_{i=1}^r u_i \equiv \sum_{i=1}^r v_i \pmod p$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Apply Theorem~\ref{thm:pigeon} with $S=T_r(A)$, of size $k^r>p$, and the
residue map $u\mapsto(\sum_i u_i)\bmod p$.
\end{proof}

For $r=2$ this is the sumset collision, for $r=3$ the $3$SUM collision.

\begin{theorem}[$r$-SUM adversary]
If $k^r\le p$ there is a residue map into $\{0,\dots,p-1\}$ injective on
$T_r(A)$: no $r$-SUM scheme with $\lvert A\rvert=k$ can be guaranteed to
collide.
\end{theorem}

\begin{corollary}[Storage monotonicity]
If $k\ge 1$, $r\le r'$ and $p<k^r$, then $p<k^{r'}$: raising the arity never
increases the storage requirement.
\end{corollary}

This is the only sense in which the hierarchy is real.

\subsection{A quantitative snapshot}

\begin{proposition}
For every natural $k$: $997<k^3 \iff k\ge 10$, and $997<k^2 \iff k\ge 32$.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
$9^3=729\le 997<1000=10^3$ and $31^2=961\le 997<1024=32^2$; monotonicity of
$k\mapsto k^m$ does the rest.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[The exponent gap, and its emptiness]
At $p=997$ the $3$SUM scheme requires $10$ stored elements where the sumset
scheme requires $32$---a $3.2\times$ improvement in storage, the promised
$p^{1/2}\to p^{1/3}$. Yet the inspected search spaces are $10^3=1000$ and
$32^2=1024$, both exceeding $997$ by the smallest possible margin and differing
from each other by $2.4\%$.
\end{corollary}

The two schemes do the same work; one merely remembers less while doing it.

\section{The \texorpdfstring{$\sqrt N$}{sqrt(N)} barrier}\label{sec:barrier}

\begin{lemma}\label{lem:sqrt}
If $q\le p$ then $\lfloor\sqrt{pq}\rfloor\le p$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
$pq\le p^2$, so $\lfloor\sqrt{pq}\rfloor\le\lfloor\sqrt{p^2}\rfloor=p$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Arity-independent cost barrier]\label{thm:cost}
Let $N=pq$ with $q\le p$ and $p\ge 1$. If a search space $S$ guarantees
collisions modulo $p$, then $\lvert S\rvert>\lfloor\sqrt N\rfloor$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Theorem~\ref{thm:collapse} gives $\lvert S\rvert>p$, and Lemma~\ref{lem:sqrt}
gives $p\ge\lfloor\sqrt N\rfloor$.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[$r$-SUM barrier]\label{cor:rsumbarrier}
For any arity $r$ and any $A$ with $p<\lvert A\rvert^r$ and $q\le p$, we have
$\lvert A\rvert^r>\lfloor\sqrt{pq}\rfloor$.
\end{corollary}

It is worth being precise about what this does and does not say. It \emph{does}
say that no scheme in this family---of any arity, over any set of integers,
with any generation rule---can be guaranteed to find a collision modulo the
larger prime factor of $N$ while inspecting at most $\sqrt N$ objects; the
bound is unconditional, non-asymptotic and non-probabilistic. It \emph{does
not} say that factoring requires $\sqrt N$ work: sieve methods do not proceed
by waiting for a residue collision and are not subject to
Theorem~\ref{thm:cost}. The theorem's value is that it draws the boundary of
the collision paradigm sharply enough to say where one must leave it.

\section{The amplitude barrier}\label{sec:amplitude}

Theorem~\ref{thm:cost} counts objects. A completely different quantity is also
stuck at $\sqrt N$: the arithmetic size of the integers manipulated. This
obstruction is invisible to the counting analysis and applies even to schemes
inspecting arbitrarily many tuples.

\begin{definition}[Sum set]
For $r\ge 0$ and finite $A$, let
$\Sigma_r(A)=\bigl\{\sum_{i=1}^r u_i : u\in T_r(A)\bigr\}$, the set of
\emph{distinct integer values} achieved as $r$-tuple sums.
\end{definition}

\begin{lemma}\label{lem:sumbound}
If every $a\in A$ satisfies $a\le M$, then every $s\in\Sigma_r(A)$ satisfies
$s\le rM$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{theorem}[Amplitude bound]\label{thm:amp}
If $A\subseteq[1,M]$ then $\lvert\Sigma_r(A)\rvert\le rM+1$, however large
$\lvert A\rvert^r$ may be.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
By Lemma~\ref{lem:sumbound}, $\Sigma_r(A)\subseteq\{0,1,\dots,rM\}$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[All collisions trivial when entries are small]
Let $A\subseteq[1,M]$ with $rM<p$. Then for any $u,v\in T_r(A)$ with
$\sum_i u_i \equiv \sum_i v_i \pmod p$ one has $\sum_i u_i=\sum_i v_i$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Suppose without loss of generality $\sum u_i<\sum v_i$. The congruence gives
$p\mid\sum v_i-\sum u_i$, a positive quantity, hence at least $p$. But both
sums lie in $[0,rM]$, so their difference is at most $rM<p$.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Amplitude barrier]\label{cor:amp}
A scheme with $A\subseteq[1,M]$ and $rM<p$ cannot factor $N=pq$ by collision,
no matter how many tuples it inspects: every collision has difference $0$ and
the reveal step returns $\gcd(0,N)=N$. Success requires $p\le rM$, i.e.\ entries
of size at least $p/r\ge\sqrt N/r$.
\end{corollary}

\begin{remark}[Structure cannot help]
Theorem~\ref{thm:amp} depends only on the interval $[1,M]$ containing $A$,
never on $A$'s additive structure. Sidon sets, geometric progressions,
smooth-number sets, and any other additive-combinatorial device produce sums
confined to the same interval and obey the same bound. One cannot arrange for a
small-entry set to have an unusually rich modular image, because the
\emph{integer} image is capped by amplitude alone.
\end{remark}

\begin{remark}[The bound is nearly attained]
Theorem~\ref{thm:amp} gives the necessary condition $p\le rM$. For the full
interval $A=\{1,\dots,M\}$ the sum set is exactly $\{r,r+1,\dots,rM\}$, of size
$r(M-1)+1$, so the counting condition $p<\lvert\Sigma_r(A)\rvert$ holds
precisely when $M\ge p/r+1$. The two conditions differ by a single additive
step, so the amplitude bound is essentially attained rather than lossy. For
$r=3$ this predicts the smallest workable entry bound
$M=\lceil p/3\rceil+1$, i.e.\ $M=5$ at $p=11$ and $M=35$ at $p=101$---values
confirmed by direct enumeration.
\end{remark}

\section{The span and coverage barriers}\label{sec:span}

\begin{definition}[Abstract collision scheme]
A \emph{scheme} consists of a finite \emph{search space} $S$, whose cardinality
$k=\lvert S\rvert$ is its cost, together with a \emph{value map}
$v:S\to\N$. Its \emph{difference set} is
$D=\{v(x)-v(y) : x,y\in S,\ v(x)\ge v(y)\}$, and the scheme \emph{reveals} $f$
from $N$ if some $d\in D$ has $d>0$ and $\gcd(d,N)=f$.
\end{definition}

\begin{lemma}\label{lem:diffs}
$\lvert D\rvert\le k^2$.
\end{lemma}

The definition is deliberately permissive: it covers sumset, $3$SUM, $r$-SUM,
structured evaluation schemes, and anything else whose output is a $\gcd$ of a
difference of two computed numbers with $N$.

\subsection{Span}

\begin{theorem}[Span barrier]\label{thm:span}
If a scheme reveals $f$ from $N$, then some $d\in D$ satisfies $d\ge f$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Take $d\in D$ with $d>0$ and $\gcd(d,N)=f$. Then $f\mid d$ and $d>0$, so
$f\le d$.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[$\sqrt N$ form]
If $N=pq$ with $q\le p$ and a scheme reveals $p$, then two of its values differ
by at least $\lfloor\sqrt N\rfloor$; in particular its largest value is at
least $\lfloor\sqrt N\rfloor$.
\end{corollary}

\begin{corollary}[Small values never factor]
If all values of a scheme are $<B$ and $B\le p$, the scheme cannot reveal $p$
from $N=pq$.
\end{corollary}

\begin{theorem}[Interval span barrier]
If all values of a scheme lie in an interval $[L,L+p)$, then any two congruent
values modulo $p$ are equal. Consequently no useful collision exists, and the
value range must be at least $p$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{remark}[Structure improves counting, never span]\label{rmk:structure}
Return to the structured-evaluation row. By Theorem~\ref{thm:structured},
confining values to a set $B$ with $\lvert B\rvert\approx p/h$ makes collisions
appear after only $\lvert B\rvert+1$ evaluations---a genuine factor-$h$ saving
over the generic $p+1$. But Theorem~\ref{thm:span} is untouched: the revealed
factor $p$ still forces two integer values at distance at least $p$. Structure
compresses the number of objects; it cannot compress the objects.
\end{remark}

\subsection{Coverage}

Could a single fixed scheme---a table of numbers computed once---factor many
semiprimes? No, by pure counting on prime divisors.

\begin{lemma}\label{lem:primepow}
Let $Q$ be a finite set of distinct primes, all $\ge P$, all dividing a
positive integer $d$. Then $P^{\lvert Q\rvert}\le d$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
The primes are distinct, so their product divides $d$; the product is at least
$P^{\lvert Q\rvert}$; and $d>0$.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}\label{cor:log}
If $P>1$ and $d>0$, then $d$ has at most $\log_P d$ distinct prime divisors
$\ge P$.
\end{corollary}

\begin{theorem}[Coverage barrier]\label{thm:coverage}
Let a scheme have $k$ search points and let $Q$ be a set of primes such that
every $p\in Q$ satisfies $p\ge P>1$ and divides some difference $d\in D$ with
$0<d\le B$. Then $\lvert Q\rvert\le\log_P(B)\,k^2$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Choose for each $p\in Q$ a witnessing difference $g(p)\in D$ with
$0<g(p)\le B$ and $p\mid g(p)$. The image $g(Q)$ lies in $D$, so
$\lvert g(Q)\rvert\le k^2$ by Lemma~\ref{lem:diffs}. Each fibre $g^{-1}(b)$
consists of distinct primes $\ge P$ dividing the single positive integer
$b\le B$, so $\lvert g^{-1}(b)\rvert\le\log_P b\le\log_P B$ by
Corollary~\ref{cor:log} and monotonicity of the logarithm. Summing over fibres,
$\lvert Q\rvert\le\log_P(B)\lvert g(Q)\rvert\le\log_P(B)k^2$.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Cost form]
A scheme required to reveal each of $T$ distinct primes $\ge P$, with all
differences bounded by $B$, must satisfy $T\le\log_P(B)k^2$, i.e.\
$k\ge\sqrt{T/\log_P B}$.
\end{corollary}

Theorem~\ref{thm:coverage} is a non-uniformity bound: it limits what
precomputation achieves. Whereas Theorem~\ref{thm:cost} says a scheme is slow
on each input, Theorem~\ref{thm:coverage} says a scheme cannot be reused across
inputs.

\section{The positive theorem}\label{sec:master}

\begin{theorem}[Master theorem for $r$-SUM collision factoring]\label{thm:master}
Let $N=pq$ with $p,q$ prime. Let $A$ be a finite set of positive integers with
$a\le M$ for all $a\in A$, and suppose
\begin{enumerate}
\item (amplitude) $rM<N$, and
\item (counting) $p<\lvert\Sigma_r(A)\rvert$.
\end{enumerate}
Then there exist $s,t\in\Sigma_r(A)$ with $t<s$ and $\gcd(s-t,\,N)=p$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Since $\lvert\Sigma_r(A)\rvert>p$, the map $x\mapsto x\bmod p$ is not
injective on $\Sigma_r(A)$; pick $s\ne t$ congruent modulo $p$ with $t<s$, so
$p\mid s-t$. Also $s\le rM<N$ by Lemma~\ref{lem:sumbound} and hypothesis~(1).
Corollary~\ref{cor:colreveal} gives $\gcd(s-t,N)=p$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Both barriers are necessary]\label{thm:both}
Let $q\le p$, $A\subseteq[1,M]$, and $p<\lvert\Sigma_r(A)\rvert$. Then
$p\le rM$ and $\lvert A\rvert^r>\lfloor\sqrt{pq}\rfloor$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
By Theorem~\ref{thm:amp}, $\lvert\Sigma_r(A)\rvert\le rM+1$, so $p<rM+1$.
Since $\Sigma_r(A)$ is an image of $T_r(A)$ we have
$\lvert\Sigma_r(A)\rvert\le\lvert A\rvert^r$, whence $p<\lvert A\rvert^r$; now
apply Corollary~\ref{cor:rsumbarrier}.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[$3$SUM cost profile]
A $3$SUM scheme against $N=pq$ with $q\le p$ requires entries of size at least
$p/3$ and inspects more than $\lfloor\sqrt N\rfloor$ triples: both costs are
$\Omega(\sqrt N)$.
\end{corollary}

\section{Algorithms}

\subsection{Sum-set collision factoring}

\textbf{Input:} a semiprime $N$, an arity $r$, an entry bound $M$.
\textbf{Output:} a nontrivial factor of $N$, or failure.
\begin{enumerate}
\item Choose $A\subseteq[1,M]$.
\item Enumerate the achieved sums $\Sigma_r(A)$ and sort them.
\item For each pair $t<s$ of achieved sums, compute $g=\gcd(s-t,N)$.
\item If $1<g<N$, output $g$.
\end{enumerate}

By Theorem~\ref{thm:master}, if $rM<N$ and $\lvert\Sigma_r(A)\rvert>p$ then
step~4 succeeds; by Theorem~\ref{thm:both} this requires $M\ge p/r$ and more
than $\sqrt N$ inspected tuples, so the procedure is $\Omega(\sqrt N)$ and,
with sorting, $O(k^r\log k^r)$ where $k=\lvert A\rvert$. Note that $p$ is never
used by the search: the residue structure modulo $p$ is invisible, and only the
final $\gcd$ test reveals whether a difference happened to be a multiple of
$p$.

\subsection{Threshold and barrier calculator}

Given $p$ (or a target $N$) and an arity $r$, one computes the storage
threshold $k^{\ast}(p,r)=\min\{k:k^r>p\}=\lfloor p^{1/r}\rfloor+1$; the work
$(k^{\ast})^r$, always exceeding $p$ and within a small factor of it; the
amplitude threshold $M^{\ast}(p,r)=\lceil p/r\rceil$, attained by the full
interval at $\lceil p/r\rceil+1$; and the span requirement
$\lfloor\sqrt N\rfloor$. The output is the hierarchy table for that instance,
exhibiting the collapse numerically.

\section{Discussion}

\textbf{A bridge between problem families.} Corollary~\ref{cor:3sum} makes
precise the sense in which $3$SUM modulo an unknown prime is a factoring
primitive: an efficient algorithm for the modular variant against adversarially
hidden moduli would break factoring. The bridge is one-directional and, as our
barriers show, load-limited.

\textbf{A design principle for cost accounting.} An improvement in one resource
(storage, $p^{1/2}\to p^{1/3}$) may be exactly compensated by no improvement at
all in another (work, always $>p$). Because Theorem~\ref{thm:collapse} is an
equivalence, this is a fact about the problem, not a limitation of an analysis.
Whenever a family of algorithms is parameterised by how cleverly the search
space is generated, it is worth asking whether the acceptance criterion depends
on generation at all. Here it does not.

\textbf{Three barriers of different type.} It is unusual for a single
$\Omega(\sqrt N)$ bound to be provable in three independent ways: counting
(Theorem~\ref{thm:cost}), amplitude and span (Corollary~\ref{cor:amp},
Theorem~\ref{thm:span}), and coverage (Theorem~\ref{thm:coverage}). Each could
in principle be circumvented separately; none can be circumvented by arity.

\textbf{What is not claimed.} None of this bears on the complexity of factoring
itself. Sub-exponential methods exist and are not collision searches. The
results delimit a paradigm, which is useful precisely because it tells the
designer where not to look.

\section{Future directions}

\begin{conjecture}[Span--coverage trade-off]
For an abstract scheme with $k$ search points and values bounded by $B$ that
reveals the larger factor of \emph{every} semiprime $N=pq$ with
$\sqrt N\in[P,2P)$, one has $k^2\log_P B\ge\pi(2P)-\pi(P)$, hence
$k\ge P^{1/2-o(1)}$: a $\sqrt N$ lower bound with no probabilistic or oracle
assumptions.
\end{conjecture}

The coverage barrier already bounds the number of large primes a fixed value
set can expose by $\log_P(B)k^2$; only a prime-counting input is needed to
convert it into an unconditional cost bound.

\begin{conjecture}[Non-uniform sets do not beat amplitude]
For every finite $A\subseteq[1,M]$ and every arity $r$, the number of distinct
residues modulo $p$ realised by $r$-tuple sums over $A$ is at most
$\min(rM+1,p)$, and the requirement $p\le rM$ for a guaranteed
factor-revealing collision cannot be improved by any choice of $A$---Sidon
sets, geometric progressions and smooth-number sets included.
\end{conjecture}

The amplitude bound depends only on the interval containing $A$, never on its
additive structure, so additive-combinatorial cleverness cannot help. Measured
interval thresholds match the predictions exactly at small $p$ ($M=5$ at
$p=11$, $M=35$ at $p=101$, both with $r=3$), so the conjecture is sharp and
would be falsified by a single counterexample set.

\begin{conjecture}[Structure beats counting, never span]
For any scheme whose values are constrained to a structured residue set $B$
with $\lvert B\rvert\approx p/h$, collisions appear after $\lvert B\rvert+1$
evaluations, yet the revealed factor still forces two integer values at
distance $\ge p$. Structure improves the collision count by the factor $h$ and
leaves the arithmetic size of the manipulated objects untouched.
\end{conjecture}

Two further directions seem worth pursuing. A \emph{probabilistic} refinement:
the collapse theorem is a worst-case guarantee, and the average-case birthday
behaviour---collisions after $\Theta(\sqrt p)$ random samples---deserves the
same arity-independence analysis, with $\sqrt p$ in place of $p$ and the
amplitude barrier unchanged. And an examination of whether any
\emph{non}-collision extraction rule evades Theorem~\ref{thm:span}, which would
identify precisely which feature of the paradigm the span barrier punishes.

\section{Conclusion}

A single greatest-common-divisor computation converts a $3$SUM solution modulo
a hidden prime into that prime, with no side conditions beyond smallness. This
makes available a family of collision-based factoring schemes, apparently
arranged in a hierarchy in which higher arity means a better exponent.

The hierarchy collapses. A collision is guaranteed exactly when the search
space exceeds the modulus---a criterion in which the arity does not
appear---so all schemes share the threshold $p+1$ and hence exceed $\sqrt N$.
Two independent barriers reach the same magnitude for different reasons: the
amplitude and span obstructions force the manipulated integers to be of size
$\sqrt N$, and the coverage obstruction forbids a fixed scheme from serving
many inputs. Once both barriers are cleared, the method provably works.

The improvement from $p^{1/2}$ to $p^{1/3}$ is real, and it is an improvement
in storage alone. The barrier does not move.

\end{document}

          f"{'> p ?':>6} | {'> sqrt(N) ?':>12}")

# Section 6 -- the span barrier
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------


def scheme_differences(values: Sequence[int]) -> Set[int]:
    """All nonnegative pairwise differences of a scheme's values."""
    return {abs(x - y) for x in values for y in values}


def demo_span(p: int = 61, q: int = 53) -> None:
    N = p * q

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Section 7 -- the coverage barrier
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------


def large_prime_divisors(d: int, P: int) -> Set[int]:
    """Distinct prime divisors of d that are at least P."""
    out: Set[int] = set()
    m, f = d, 2
    while f * f <= m:
        if m % f == 0:
            if f >= P:
                out.add(f)
            while m % f == 0:
                m //= f
        f += 1
    if m > 1 and m >= P:
        out.add(m)
    return out


def demo_coverage(k: int = 12, B: int = 10 ** 6, P: int = 100, seed: int = 7) -> None:
    print(f"\n[7] Coverage barrier: k = {k} search points, values < B = {B}, "
          f"P = {P}")
    # deterministic pseudo-random values, no external dependencies
    state = seed
    values: List[int] = []
    for _ in range(k):
        state = (1103515245 * state + 12345) % (2 ** 31)
        values.append(state % B)
    diffs = {d for d in scheme_differences(values) if 0 < d <= B}
    exposed: Set[int] = set()
    for d in diffs:
        exposed |= large_prime_divisors(d, P)
    bound = int(math.log(B, P)) * k ** 2
    print(f"    pairwise differences: {len(diffs)} (bound k^2 = {k ** 2})")
    print(f"    distinct primes >= {P} exposed: {len(exposed)}")
    print(f"    coverage bound log_P(B) * k^2 = {bound}")
    print(f"    bound respected: {len(exposed) <= bound}")
    assert len(exposed) <= bound


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Section 8 -- end-to-end collision factoring
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------


def collision_factor(N: int, r: int, M: int) -> Optional[Tuple[int, int, int]]:
    """Factor N by an r-SUM collision search over A = {1, ..., M}.

    Returns (s, t, factor) where s > t are achieved r-tuple sums with
    gcd(s - t, N) a nontrivial factor, or None if no useful collision exists.
    Note that p is never used by the search: only the final gcd test looks
    at N.
    """
    sums = sorted(sum_set(list(range(1, M + 1)), r))
    for i, s in enumerate(sums):
        for t in sums[:i]:
            g = gcd(s - t, N)
            if 1 < g < N:
                return s, t, g
    return None


def demo_end_to_end() -> None:
    print("\n[8] End-to-end r-SUM collision factoring")
    cases: List[Tuple[int, int, int, int]] = [
        (11, 13, 3, 6),     # N = 143
        (23, 19, 3, 12),    # N = 437
        (31, 29, 2, 20),    # N = 899
        (41, 37, 4, 14),    # N = 1517
    ]
    for p, q, r, M in cases:
        N = p * q
        res = collision_factor(N, r, M)
        if res is None:
            print(f"    N = {N:5d}, r = {r}, M = {M:3d}: no useful collision "
                  f"(amplitude barrier: r*M = {r * M} vs p = {p})")
        else:
            s, t, g = res
            print(f"    N = {N:5d} = {p}*{q}, r = {r}, M = {M:3d}: "
                  f"sums {s} and {t}, gcd({s - t}, {N}) = {g}  "
                  f"[{'correct' if N % g == 0 and 1 < g < N else 'ERROR'}]")
    print("    below the amplitude threshold the search provably fails:")
    p, q, r, M = 41, 37, 3, 5
    N = p * q
    res = collision_factor(N, r, M)
    print(f"    N = {N}, r = {r}, M = {M}: r*M = {r * M} < p = {p}  ->  "
          f"result = {res}")


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Main
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------


def main() -> None:
    print("=" * 74)
    print("THE 3SUM-BIRTHDAY-BOUND HIERARCHY -- numerical demonstrations")
    print("=" * 74)

    print("\n[1] The reveal lemma")
    for p, q in ((11, 13), (17, 19), (61, 53)):
        assert check_reveal_lemma(p, q)
        assert check_no_double_divisibility(p, q)

    demo_census()
    demo_collapse()
    hierarchy_table(1009, 997)
    demo_exponent_gap_997()
    demo_amplitude()
    demo_amplitude_thresholds()
    demo_span()
    demo_coverage()
    demo_end_to_end()

    print("\n" + "=" * 74)
    print("All demonstrations completed; every assertion held.")
    print("=" * 74)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

def storage_threshold(p: int, r: int) -> int:
    """Smallest k with k**r > p."""
    if r == 0:
        raise ValueError("arity must be positive")
    k = max(1, round(p ** (1.0 / r)))
    while k ** r <= p:
        k += 1
    while k > 1 and (k - 1) ** r > p:
        k -= 1
    return k


def hierarchy_table(p: int, q: int, arities: Iterable[int] = (2, 3, 4, 5, 6)) -> None:
    N = p * q
    print(f"\n[4] Hierarchy table for N = {N} = {p} * {q}, "
          f"floor(sqrt(N)) = {isqrt(N)}")
    print(f"    {'arity r':>7} | {'stored k':>10} | {'inspected k^r':>16} | "
          f"{'> p ?':>6} | {'> sqrt(N) ?':>12}")
    print("    " + "-" * 64)
    for r in arities:
        k = storage_threshold(p, r)
        work = k ** r
        print(f"    {r:>7} | {k:>10} | {work:>16} | "
              f"{str(work > p):>6} | {str(work > isqrt(N)):>12}")
    print("    storage shrinks like p^(1/r); inspected tuples never drop below p.")


def demo_exponent_gap_997() -> None:

    k2, k3 = storage_threshold(p, 2), storage_threshold(p, 3)
    print(f"    sumset (r=2): smallest k with k^2 > {p} is k = {k2}, "

def sum_set(A: Sequence[int], r: int) -> Set[int]:
    """All distinct integer sums of r-tuples drawn (with repetition) from A."""
    sums: Set[int] = {0}
    for _ in range(r):
        sums = {s + a for s in sums for a in A}
    return sums

def scheme_differences(values: Sequence[int]) -> Set[int]:
    """All nonnegative pairwise differences of a scheme's values."""
    return {abs(x - y) for x in values for y in values}

def large_prime_divisors(d: int, P: int) -> Set[int]:
    """Distinct prime divisors of d that are at least P."""
    out: Set[int] = set()
    m, f = d, 2
    while f * f <= m:
        if m % f == 0:
            if f >= P:
                out.add(f)
            while m % f == 0:
                m //= f
        f += 1
    if m > 1 and m >= P:
        out.add(m)
    return out


def demo_coverage(k: int = 12, B: int = 10 ** 6, P: int = 100, seed: int = 7) -> None:
    print(f"\n[7] Coverage barrier: k = {k} search points, values < B = {B}, "
          f"P = {P}")
    # deterministic pseudo-random values, no external dependencies
    state = seed
    values: List[int] = []
    for _ in range(k):
        state = (1103515245 * state + 12345) % (2 ** 31)
        values.append(state % B)
    diffs = {d for d in scheme_differences(values) if 0 < d <= B}
    exposed: Set[int] = set()
    for d in diffs:
        exposed |= large_prime_divisors(d, P)
    bound = int(math.log(B, P)) * k ** 2
    print(f"    pairwise differences: {len(diffs)} (bound k^2 = {k ** 2})")
    print(f"    distinct primes >= {P} exposed: {len(exposed)}")
    print(f"    coverage bound log_P(B) * k^2 = {bound}")
    print(f"    bound respected: {len(exposed) <= bound}")
    assert len(exposed) <= bound

def collision_factor(N: int, r: int, M: int) -> Optional[Tuple[int, int, int]]:
    """Factor N by an r-SUM collision search over A = {1, ..., M}.

    Returns (s, t, factor) where s > t are achieved r-tuple sums with
    gcd(s - t, N) a nontrivial factor, or None if no useful collision exists.
    Note that p is never used by the search: only the final gcd test looks
    at N.
    """
    sums = sorted(sum_set(list(range(1, M + 1)), r))
    for i, s in enumerate(sums):
        for t in sums[:i]:
            g = gcd(s - t, N)
            if 1 < g < N:
                return s, t, g
    return None

def adversarial_map(space: List[int], p: int) -> Optional[Dict[int, int]]:
    """An injective residue map on `space`, or None if none can exist."""
    if len(space) > p:
        return None                      # pigeonhole forbids it
    return {x: i for i, x in enumerate(space)}


def has_collision(colouring: Dict[int, int]) -> bool:
    return len(set(colouring.values())) < len(colouring)


def random_map(space: List[int], p: int, rng: random.Random) -> Dict[int, int]:
    return {x: rng.randrange(p) for x in space}


def tuple_space_size(k: int, r: int) -> int:
    return k ** r


def tournament(p: int, trials: int = 400, seed: int = 11) -> None:
    rng = random.Random(seed)

          f"{'random maps that collide':>26}")
    print("-" * 68)
    for size in (5, 10, 20, p - 1, p, p + 1, 2 * p):
        space = list(range(size))
        adv = adversarial_map(space, p)
        collided = sum(1 for _ in range(trials)
                       if has_collision(random_map(space, p, rng)))
        print(f"{size:>6} {str(adv is not None):>17} "
              f"{str(adv is None):>13} {collided:>10}/{trials:<15}")

    print(f"{'arity r':>8} {'stored k':>9} {'|S| = k^r':>11} "
          f"{'guaranteed?':>13}")
    print("-" * 46)
    for r in (2, 3, 4, 5):
        k = 1
        while tuple_space_size(k, r) <= p:
            k += 1
        for kk in (k - 1, k):
            size = tuple_space_size(kk, r)
            print(f"{r:>8} {kk:>9} {size:>11} "
                  f"{str(size > p):>13}")
    print("\nOnly |S| matters. Two schemes of different arity with the same |S|")
    print("succeed or fail together; the arity changes only the stored count k.")


def average_case_note(p: int, samples: int = 2000, seed: int = 5) -> None:
    """Where the *first* random collision typically appears (birthday effect)."""
    rng = random.Random(seed)
    firsts: List[int] = []
    for _ in range(samples):
        seen = set()
        n = 0
        while True:
            n += 1
            v = rng.randrange(p)
            if v in seen:
                firsts.append(n)
                break
            seen.add(v)
    mean = sum(firsts) / len(firsts)
    print(f"\naverage-case: with random values mod p = {p}, the first collision "
          f"appears after {mean:.1f} draws")
    print(f"  (the birthday scale is sqrt(pi*p/2) = {(3.14159265 * p / 2) ** 0.5:.1f})")
    print(f"  but the worst-case guarantee still requires {p + 1} draws.")

def sum_set(M: int, r: int) -> List[int]:

    barrier, is guaranteed whenever r*M < p.
    Complexity: O(r*M) distinct sums, O((r*M)^2) gcd tests in this naive form.

    sums = sum_set(M, r)
    for i, s in enumerate(sums):
        for t in sums[:i]:

            if 1 < g < N:

    return None


def rsum_collision_factor_fast(N: int, r: int, M: int) -> Optional[Tuple[int, int, int]]:
    """Same output, exploiting the structure of the sum set.

    gcd count from quadratic to linear in the amplitude.

    sums = sum_set(M, r)

        if 1 < g < N:

    return None

      "code": """"Algorithm 3: coverage audit for a fixed collision scheme.

A fixed scheme is a finite list of values v_1, ..., v_k. It can only ever
reveal a prime f from some N if f divides one of its at most k^2 pairwise
differences. Since a positive integer d <= B has at most log_P(B) distinct
prime divisors that are >= P, the total number of large primes a fixed scheme
can expose is at most log_P(B) * k^2.

This audit enumerates the primes actually exposed and compares the count with
the bound, certifying that no precomputed table of moderate size can factor
many semiprimes with large factors.

Complexity: O(k^2) differences, each factored by trial division in

from __future__ import annotations

import math
from typing import Dict, List, Sequence, Set


def pairwise_differences(values: Sequence[int]) -> Set[int]:
    """All strictly positive pairwise differences of the scheme's values."""
    return {abs(x - y) for x in values for y in values if x != y}


def large_prime_divisors(d: int, P: int) -> Set[int]:
    """Distinct prime divisors of d that are at least P."""
    out: Set[int] = set()
    m, f = d, 2
    while f * f <= m:
        if m % f == 0:
            if f >= P:
                out.add(f)
            while m % f == 0:
                m //= f
        f += 1
    if m > 1 and m >= P:
        out.add(m)
    return out


def coverage_audit(values: Sequence[int], P: int) -> Dict[str, object]:
    """Compare the primes a fixed scheme exposes with the coverage bound."""
    k = len(values)
    diffs = pairwise_differences(values)
    B = max(diffs) if diffs else 1
    exposed: Set[int] = set()
    for d in diffs:
        exposed |= large_prime_divisors(d, P)
    bound = int(math.log(B, P)) * k ** 2 if B > 1 and P > 1 else 0
    return {
        "search_points": k,
        "distinct_differences": len(diffs),
        "difference_bound_B": B,
        "primes_exposed": len(exposed),
        "coverage_bound": bound,
        "bound_respected": len(exposed) <= bound,
        "semiprimes_coverable": len(exposed),
    }

def integer_root(p: int, r: int) -> int:
    k = max(1, int(round(p ** (1.0 / r))))
    while k ** r > p:
        k -= 1
    while (k + 1) ** r <= p:

    return k

def make_figure(p: int = 101, m_max: int = 60, r_max: int = 8) -> None:
    Ms = np.arange(1, m_max + 1)
    rs = np.arange(1, r_max + 1)

    tuples = np.zeros((len(rs), len(Ms)))

    for i, r in enumerate(rs):
        for j, M in enumerate(Ms):
            distinct_sums = r * (M - 1) + 1
            if r * M < p:
                grid[i, j] = 0.0          # DEAD
            elif distinct_sums <= p:
                grid[i, j] = 0.5          # BLIND
            else:

            tuples[i, j] = r * np.log10(max(M, 1))

                 f"red = every collision trivial, green = factor guaranteed")
    ax.legend(loc="upper right")
    fig.tight_layout()
    fig.savefig("amplitude_phase.png", dpi=160)
    print("wrote amplitude_phase.png")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    make_figure()

### A guided tour of the 3SUM–birthday-bound hierarchy and why it collapses

---

## 1. A trick you can do in your head

Take $N = 143$. It is a product of two primes and I will not tell you which. Pick three distinct numbers between $1$ and $12$ — say $2$, $4$ and $5$ — and add them: $2+4+5 = 11$. Now compute $\gcd(11, 143)$.

You get $11$. That *is* one of the primes. The other is $13$.

This is not luck. Every triple $a<b<c$ from $\{1,\dots,12\}$ whose sum happens to be a multiple of $11$ hands you the factor, and there are exactly $20$ of them. Even better: *no* triple in this range can fail in the dangerous way, by being a multiple of both primes at once. The reason is a two-line theorem.

> **Reveal Lemma.** Let $N = pq$ with $p, q$ prime. If $0 < s < N$ and $p \mid s$, then $\gcd(s, N) = p$.

<details>
<summary><b>Click to reveal the proof — and the hypothesis everybody adds but nobody needs</b></summary>

Let $g = \gcd(s, N)$. Since $p$ divides both $s$ and $N$, $p \mid g$; write $g = pd$. Since $g \mid pq$, we get $d \mid q$, so $d = 1$ or $d = q$ because $q$ is prime.

- If $d = 1$, then $g = p$ and we are done.
- If $d = q$, then $g = N$, and $g \mid s$ gives $N \mid s$. But $s$ is positive and smaller than $N$. Contradiction.

Textbooks usually state this with an extra hypothesis: "provided $q \nmid s$." The proof shows it is **redundant** — it follows from $s < N$. If both primes divided $s$, then $pq = N$ would divide $s$, forcing $s \ge N$. Smallness alone excludes the bad case.

This is exactly why the "divisible by both" column of any experiment with small triples is empty: it is empty *by theorem*, not by luck.
</details>

The lemma turns factoring into a search: you no longer need to guess $p$. You just need to stumble on a number below $N$ that happens to be a multiple of $p$ — and a single greatest-common-divisor computation tells you when you have.

Learn more about [the greatest common divisor and the Euclidean algorithm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euclidean_algorithm).

---

## 2. Enter the birthday paradox

How do you stumble on multiples of an *invisible* prime? You do not aim at them. You generate lots of numbers and wait for two of them to leave the same remainder modulo $p$. Their difference is then a multiple of $p$ — and by the reveal lemma, one $\gcd$ finishes the job.

This is the [birthday problem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birthday_problem) wearing a number-theoretic hat: in a room of $23$ people two probably share a birthday, and among enough integers two must share a residue.

The design question is: *how do we generate many integers cheaply?* Here is the ladder that suggests itself.

| scheme | search space | stored elements needed |
|---|---|---|
| sumset, $a+b \equiv c+d$ | $k^2$ | $k \sim p^{1/2}$ |
| 3SUM, $a+b+c \equiv d+e+f$ | $k^3$ | $k \sim p^{1/3}$ |
| $r$-SUM | $k^r$ | $k \sim p^{1/r}$ |

The exponent improves. It looks like a hierarchy of ever-better factoring algorithms. Let us find out whether it is.

---

## 3. Play with the machine yourself

Before any more theory, get your hands on the object. The laboratory below builds the whole scheme in front of you: choose the two hidden primes, the arity $r$, and the bound $M$ on the numbers you are allowed to use. It shows every achieved sum coloured by its residue modulo $p$, finds the first collision, and runs the $\gcd$.

**Things to try:**
1. Set $p = 41$, $r = 3$, and slide $M$ up from $1$. Nothing happens for a long time — then, suddenly, at $M = 15$ the machine factors. Look at the colour strip: below the threshold, *every colour is different*.
2. Now set $r = 1$ and raise $M$ until it works ($M = 42$). Then set $r = 6$ and do it again ($M = 8$). The entry bound collapses, but the product $r \cdot M$ lands just above $p$ both times — the scheme switches on when the *span* of its values reaches $p$, never before.
3. Set $r = 8$ and $M = 4$. The scheme inspects $4^8 = 65{,}536$ tuples and still fails. **More tuples do not help.**

{{interactive_demo:0}}

That third experiment is the whole story in miniature, and it has a name.

## 4. The amplitude barrier: small numbers cannot factor

If your building blocks all lie in $\{1,\dots,M\}$, then every sum of $r$ of them lies between $r$ and $rM$. There are at most $rM+1$ *distinct* sums, no matter that there are $M^r$ tuples.

Now suppose $rM < p$. Two sums congruent modulo $p$ must differ by a multiple of $p$ — but no two of our sums are that far apart. So they are **equal**. The collision is trivial, the difference is $0$, and $\gcd(0, N) = N$: no factor.

> **Amplitude Barrier.** A collision scheme drawing entries from $[1,M]$ at arity $r$ cannot factor $N = pq$ unless $p \le rM$. Below that line, every collision it will ever find is worthless, however many tuples it inspects.

<details>
<summary><b>Why additive cleverness cannot rescue you</b></summary>

The bound $|\Sigma_r(A)| \le rM+1$ depends only on the *interval* containing $A$ — never on $A$'s additive structure. Sidon sets, geometric progressions, smooth numbers: all of them produce sums inside $[r, rM]$, so all of them obey the same cap. One cannot engineer a small-entry set with an unusually rich modular image, because the *integer* image is capped by amplitude alone.

The bound is essentially attained. For the full interval $A = \{1,\dots,M\}$ the sum set is exactly $\{r, r+1, \dots, rM\}$, of size $r(M-1)+1$, so the scheme switches on precisely at $M \ge p/r + 1$. At $p = 11, r = 3$ that predicts $M = 5$; at $p = 101, r = 3$ it predicts $M = 35$. Both match direct enumeration exactly.
</details>

The phase diagram below shows the barrier as a landscape. Red: every collision trivial. Green: a factor is guaranteed. The thin black curves are contours of constant tuple count $M^r$ — notice how they cut *across* the boundary. Walking along a contour (doing more work) never takes you from red to green. Only walking right (using bigger numbers) does.

{{visualization:1}}

---

## 5. The collapse: the theorem that flattens the ladder

Now for the main event. Forget sums, forget arity. Abstract everything away and keep only this: a finite search space $S$, and some assignment of residues modulo $p$ to its points.

> **Collapse Theorem.** A collision is guaranteed on $S$ — meaning: for *every* assignment of residues in $\{0,\dots,p-1\}$, two distinct points of $S$ share a residue — **if and only if** $p < |S|$.

Read the criterion again. It mentions $|S|$, the number of inspected objects. It does not mention the arity. It does not mention how the tuples were built. It does not mention the additive structure of anything.

<details>
<summary><b>Click to reveal both directions of the proof</b></summary>

**($\Leftarrow$) Pigeonhole.** If $|S| > p$, then any map from $S$ into the $p$-element set $\{0,\dots,p-1\}$ fails to be injective. Two points collide.

**($\Rightarrow$) The adversary.** If $|S| \le p$, embed $S$ injectively into $\{0,\dots,p-1\}$ and use that embedding as the residue map (send everything outside $S$ to $0$). This map has *no* collision on $S$, so the guarantee fails.

The second direction is what makes the result a genuine lower bound rather than an artefact of one analysis: for every search space of size at most $p$, there is a concrete residue assignment that defeats it.
</details>

Combine this with a fact about semiprimes: if $N = pq$ with $q \le p$, then $N \le p^2$, so $p \ge \sqrt N$. We get:

> **The Barrier.** Any collision scheme guaranteed to expose the larger factor of $N = pq$ must inspect more than $\sqrt N$ objects — at *every* arity.

Watch it happen. In the explorer below, the left column (stored elements) genuinely falls as you raise the arity. The right column (objects inspected) does not budge.

{{interactive_demo:1}}

And here it is as a picture, at $p \approx 10^6$: two panels, one showing a real improvement and one showing none at all.

## 6. The exponent gap, in one concrete number

Take $p = 997$.

- Sumset scheme: needs $k \ge 32$, because $31^2 = 961 \le 997 < 1024 = 32^2$.
- 3SUM scheme: needs $k \ge 10$, because $9^3 = 729 \le 997 < 1000 = 10^3$.

Storage falls by a factor of $3.2$ — exactly the promised $p^{1/2} \to p^{1/3}$. And the work? $32^2 = 1024$ versus $10^3 = 1000$. A difference of $2.4\%$.

The two schemes do the same amount of work. One of them merely remembers less while doing it.

The tournament below plays the adversary game explicitly, and also shows the *average*-case behaviour for contrast: random values collide after about $\sqrt{\pi p/2} \approx 40$ draws at $p = 997$, but the worst-case guarantee still needs $998$.

{{demo:1}}

---

## 7. Two more walls, for entirely different reasons

What makes $\sqrt N$ convincing as the true home of this paradigm is that *three independent arguments* reach it.

<details>
<summary><b>The span barrier — the numbers themselves must be big</b></summary>

Strip a scheme down to a finite list of values, with factors extracted as $\gcd$ of differences with $N$. If such a scheme reveals a factor $f$, then $f$ divides one of its positive differences, so **some two values differ by at least $f$**. One line of proof.

For $f = p \ge \sqrt N$, this says: any scheme that factors a semiprime must manipulate numbers spanning at least $\sqrt N$. A scheme whose values all live below $\sqrt N$ cannot reveal the larger factor, no matter how many values it has.

This has a pretty consequence for the exotic end of the hierarchy. Some schemes confine their values to a structured subset $B$ of the residues, of size roughly $p/h$ for a structural parameter $h$. Such a scheme *does* beat the counting threshold — collisions appear after $|B|+1$ evaluations, a factor of $h$ sooner, since the general threshold is the size of the *value set*. But the span barrier is untouched. **Structure compresses the number of objects; it cannot compress the objects.**
</details>

<details>
<summary><b>The coverage barrier — no fixed table is universal</b></summary>

Could one precompute a magic list of numbers that factors everything? No.

A scheme with $k$ search points has at most $k^2$ pairwise differences. A positive integer $d \le B$ has at most $\log_P B$ distinct prime divisors that are $\ge P$ — because $s$ such primes multiply to something $\ge P^s$, which must divide $d$. So the total number of large primes a fixed scheme can *ever* expose is at most
$$\log_P(B)\cdot k^2.$$
A scheme required to crack $T$ different semiprimes with larger factor $\ge P$ therefore needs $k \ge \sqrt{T/\log_P B}$.

Whereas the collapse theorem says a scheme is slow on each input, this says a scheme cannot be reused across inputs. Together they close the two obvious escape routes.
</details>

{{algorithm:2}}

---

## 8. The positive result: it does work, once you pay

None of this is pure negation. Pay both prices and the method is provably correct.

> **Master Theorem.** Let $N = pq$ with $p,q$ prime, let $A \subseteq [1,M]$ with $rM < N$, and suppose the set of $r$-tuple sums over $A$ has more than $p$ elements. Then two achieved sums $t < s$ satisfy $\gcd(s-t, N) = p$.

Notice what the algorithm does *not* need: it never uses $p$. The residue structure modulo the hidden prime is invisible throughout the search; only the final $\gcd$ test looks at $N$ and discovers that a difference happened to be a multiple of $p$.

## 10. What to take away

- A $3$SUM instance taken modulo an unknown prime factor of $N$ is a **factoring oracle** — a real bridge between a canonical problem of [fine-grained complexity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fine-grained_complexity) and the canonical problem of [public-key cryptography](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/RSA_cryptosystem).
- Raising the arity is a genuine improvement — **in storage only**. The number of objects inspected is pinned at $p+1$ by an *if-and-only-if* theorem, so this is a fact about the problem, not a limitation of an analysis.
- Three independent barriers — counting, amplitude/span, and coverage — all land at $\sqrt N$ for different reasons. That robustness is why $\sqrt N$ is the true home of the collision paradigm.
- The general lesson: an exponent measures *one* resource. Improving it while three others stay frozen is not progress, it is bookkeeping. Always ask whether the acceptance criterion of your method mentions the thing you just optimised. Here, famously, it does not.

The record-setting factoring methods of today are sieves, not collision searches, and they run far below $\sqrt N$. That is not a contradiction — it is the point. The birthday paradox is a beautiful engine, but it is bolted to the floor. To go faster, you have to get off it.
